title: Logistic regression, predicting yes or no
html:
Purpose. Many business questions have a yes or no answer: will this customer repay, accept the offer, churn? Logistic regression is the standard first model for them. It is easy to explain, hard to beat as a baseline, and it is also the building block of neural networks.

Key ideas

  • Despite its name, logistic regression is a classification model. It outputs a probability between 0 and 1.
  • It takes the same weighted sum as linear regression, z = w . x + b, and squeezes it through the sigmoid function.
  • The decision boundary is where z = 0, which is where the probability is 0.5.
  • The 0.5 cut-off is a choice, not a law. You can move it.

9.1 Why not a straight line?

Ng's example is a tumour that is benign (0) or malignant (1), predicted from its size. You could fit a straight line to those 0s and 1s and call anything above 0.5 malignant. It works on tidy data, but it breaks for two reasons (Ng, video 31):

  • Add one very large tumour far to the right. The line tilts to chase it, the 0.5 crossing moves, and some tumours that were classified correctly are now wrong. One outlier should not rewrite your rule.
  • The line produces numbers like -0.4 and 1.7. They are not probabilities and mean nothing.

We need a curve that stays between 0 and 1 and flattens at both ends.

9.2 The sigmoid

g(z)=11+e−zfw⃗,b(x⃗)=g(w⃗⋅x⃗+b)g(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}} \qquad f_{\vec{w},b}(\vec{x}) = g(\vec{w} \cdot \vec{x} + b)

For a very large z the sigmoid is close to 1. For a very large negative z it is close to 0. At z = 0 it is exactly 0.5. Some values: g(-3) = 0.047, g(-1) = 0.269, g(0) = 0.5, g(1) = 0.731, g(3) = 0.953.

Read the model's output as a probability: if f(x) = 0.7, the model says there is a 70% chance that y = 1 for this input (and so a 30% chance that y = 0).

9.3 The decision boundary

To turn the probability into a yes or no, use a threshold, usually 0.5. The sigmoid is at least 0.5 exactly when z is at least 0, so the model predicts 1 when w . x + b is at least 0. The set of inputs where w . x + b = 0 is the decision boundary: a line when there are two features.

Take w = [1, 1] and b = -3. The boundary is x1 + x2 = 3.

Input x z = x1 + x2 - 3 Probability Prediction
[1, 1] -1 0.269 0
[2, 2] 1 0.731 1
[3, 0] 0 0.5 on the boundary

Straight boundaries are not the limit. If you feed the model squared features, such as x1 squared and x2 squared (Chapter 8), then with weights 1 and 1 and b = -1 the boundary x1 squared + x2 squared = 1 is a circle: points inside are class 0, points outside class 1. The model is still logistic regression; only the features changed.

9.4 Odds and log-odds

Beyond the videos (this is the statistician's view, as in StatQuest). The odds of an event are p divided by (1 - p): a probability of 0.8 is odds of 4 to 1. The logarithm of the odds is the log-odds (or logit): ln 4 = 1.386.

Here is the neat fact: z = w . x + b is exactly the log-odds. Logistic regression is linear regression on the log-odds, and the sigmoid just turns log-odds back into a probability. This gives you a way to read the weights: each increase of 1 in feature j multiplies the odds by e to the power w_j. A weight of 0.5 multiplies the odds by 1.649, so "4 to 1" becomes about "6.6 to 1", all else equal.

9.5 The threshold is a choice

The default 0.5 treats both mistakes as equally bad. In lending they are not. Approving a loan that defaults costs far more than declining a good applicant. You can lower the threshold to flag more risky cases (catching more bad loans, with more false alarms) or raise it to be stricter. Chapter 12 shows how to choose with numbers.

9.6 More than two classes

Beyond the videos. With more than two classes (the Gmail tabs example) the sigmoid is replaced by the softmax function. It turns one score per class into probabilities that add up to 1. You will meet it again as the last layer of most neural networks.

import numpy as np

def sigmoid(z):
    return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))

print(sigmoid(np.array([-3, -1, 0, 1, 3])).round(3))      # [0.047 0.269 0.5   0.731 0.953]

w, b = np.array([1.0, 1.0]), -3.0
for x in ([1, 1], [2, 2], [3, 0]):
    p = sigmoid(np.dot(w, x) + b)
    print(x, round(p, 3), "->", int(p >= 0.5))
# [1, 1] 0.269 -> 0
# [2, 2] 0.731 -> 1
# [3, 0] 0.5 -> 1   (exactly on the boundary: the >= rule says 1)

p = 0.8
print(round(p / (1 - p), 2), round(np.log(p / (1 - p)), 3))   # 4.0 1.386  odds and log-odds

Loan example. The probability that an offer is accepted is the sigmoid of w1 x amount + w2 x terms + w3 x credit score + b. A probability of 0.83 means "about 83 of 100 offers like this are accepted". You can rank offers by it, or turn it into a decision with a threshold, and a customer-facing explanation can use the weights: a larger amount lowers the odds of acceptance by a certain factor.

Common mistakes

  • Using linear regression on a 0 or 1 target.
  • Thinking the model output is a certainty. It is a probability, and only as good as its calibration (Chapter 12).
  • Treating 0.5 as sacred.
  • Forgetting to scale the features before training (Chapter 8).

Check yourself

  • Compute sigmoid(0) and say what it means.
  • For w = [2, -1], b = 1 and x = [1, 3], what is z, and what does the model predict?
  • Why can a straight line not be the model for yes or no data?
  • A probability is 0.2. What are the odds?
Show answers

(1) 0.5: the model is undecided, and the input is on the decision boundary. (2) z = 2 x 1 - 1 x 3 + 1 = 0, so the probability is 0.5, exactly on the boundary. (3) It gives values outside 0 and 1, and a single outlier can move its threshold. (4) 0.2 / 0.8 = 0.25, which is 1 to 4.
